title: Ezekiel 33:10–20
context: The LORD tells the prophet to answer the house of Israel, who say, “Our transgressions and our sins are on us, and we pine away in them. How then can we live?” (33:10). The answer is an oath: “I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live”, followed by the cry “Turn, turn from your evil ways!” (33:11). The LORD then restates the cases of the righteous who trusts in his righteousness and commits iniquity, and the wicked who turns and does “that which is lawful and right” (33:12–16, 33:18–19), and he answers the complaint that “The way of the Lord is not fair” (33:17, 33:20). Much of this restates 18:21–32 (compare 18:23, 18:25, and 18:29–32), and it also echoes 3:20–21. Both traditions affirm that the LORD takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked and that the call to turn is sincere. They differ on how that call relates to God’s purpose, which the 1 Timothy 2:4 box treats, and on what a righteous person’s turning away implies. How directly these verses speak to final salvation, rather than to life and death within Ezekiel’s covenant setting, is debated; the wider question of falling away is treated at Hebrews 6:4 and Hebrews 6:6, and is not settled here.

verses.text: “You, son of man, tell the house of Israel: ‘You say this, “Our transgressions and our sins are on us, and we pine away in them. How then can we live?” ’
verses.arminianNotes: The house of Israel says, “Our transgressions and our sins are on us, and we pine away in them. How then can we live?” Arminian readers note that the people’s despair is met with a call to turn, not with silence. The question invites the answer of 33:11.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear honest conviction of sin that has turned toward despair, and they see the LORD answering it with his own word of life. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the setting for the oath that follows, and both see in it the burden of guilt the gospel addresses.

verses.text: Tell them, ‘ “As I live,” says the Lord GOD, “I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live. Turn, turn from your evil ways! For why will you die, house of Israel?” ’
verses.arminianNotes: “As I live,” says the Lord GOD, “I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live.” Arminian readers hear God’s sincere desire that every sinner turn and live; the 1 Timothy 2:4 box treats this question, and see 2 Peter 3:9. The cry “Turn, turn from your evil ways!” is a real offer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers affirm without reservation that God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked and that the call “Turn, turn from your evil ways!” is sincere. Many distinguish God’s revealed or preceptive will, which commands and invites all to turn, from his decretive will, as the discussion at 1 Timothy 2:4 records. Shared ground: both traditions hear the oath as a genuine plea, as at 18:23 and 18:32.

verses.text: “You, son of man, tell the children of your people, ‘The righteousness of the righteous will not deliver him in the day of his disobedience. And as for the wickedness of the wicked, he will not fall by it in the day that he turns from his wickedness; neither will he who is righteous be able to live by it in the day that he sins.
verses.arminianNotes: “The righteousness of the righteous will not deliver him in the day of his disobedience”, and the wicked “will not fall by it in the day that he turns from his wickedness”. Arminian readers see a real righteousness that can be abandoned, and a real turning that brings life. Whether this speaks of final salvation is debated; the wider question of falling away is treated at Hebrews 6:4 and Hebrews 6:6, and is not settled here.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers commonly read the righteousness here as outward or covenantal, or read the warning as one of the means by which God keeps his people persevering, while affirming the plain point that past conduct is no shelter for present rebellion. Shared ground: both traditions take the warning seriously; the wider question of falling away is treated at Hebrews 6:4 and Hebrews 6:6, and is not settled here.

verses.text: When I tell the righteous that he will surely live, if he trusts in his righteousness and commits iniquity, none of his righteous deeds will be remembered; but he will die in his iniquity that he has committed.
verses.arminianNotes: If the righteous “trusts in his righteousness and commits iniquity, none of his righteous deeds will be remembered”. Arminian readers note the warning against presuming on a past record, and they see a genuine possibility of turning away. The wider question of falling away is treated at Hebrews 6:4 and Hebrews 6:6, and is not settled here.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the man in view “trusts in his righteousness”, and many see self-reliance exposed rather than a living trust in the LORD, while others read the warning as a means of perseverance. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a sober warning; the wider question of falling away is treated at Hebrews 6:4 and Hebrews 6:6, and is not settled here.

verses.text: Again, when I say to the wicked, “You will surely die,” if he turns from his sin and does that which is lawful and right,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says to the wicked, “You will surely die,” yet “if he turns from his sin and does that which is lawful and right,” a different outcome follows. Arminian readers note that the sentence announced is not the last word for one who turns. The warning itself opens a door.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the threat of death as a warning that calls for repentance, and they see such turning as the fruit of grace (compare 36:26). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse, as at 18:21 and 18:27, as holding out life to the wicked who turn.

verses.text: if the wicked restore the pledge, give again that which he had taken by robbery, walk in the statutes of life, committing no iniquity, he will surely live. He will not die.
verses.arminianNotes: The turning is concrete: the wicked will “restore the pledge, give again that which he had taken by robbery, walk in the statutes of life”. Arminian readers note that repentance reaches into restitution and daily conduct. Then “he will surely live. He will not die.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that true repentance shows itself in a changed life, including making things right with a neighbor. Shared ground: both traditions read “the statutes of life” as the way of life the LORD gives, and neither reads the verse as earning life by restitution.

verses.text: None of his sins that he has committed will be remembered against him. He has done that which is lawful and right. He will surely live.
verses.arminianNotes: “None of his sins that he has committed will be remembered against him.” Arminian readers see the fullness of forgiveness for the one who turns: his past is no longer counted, and “He will surely live.” Mercy is as real as the warning.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s gracious forgetting of sin, a theme both traditions celebrate, as at 18:22. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as good news for the despairing people of 33:10, who asked how they could live under their sins.

verses.text: “ ‘Yet the children of your people say, “The way of the Lord is not fair;” but as for them, their way is not fair.
verses.arminianNotes: The people say, “The way of the Lord is not fair;” but the LORD answers that “their way is not fair.” Arminian readers note that the people accuse God of injustice, and the LORD turns the charge back on them. His dealings are fair because he responds to each person’s turning.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the LORD defends his justice openly rather than retreating into mystery here. Shared ground: both traditions affirm that God’s judgments are right and that the fault lies with the people, as in the parallel complaint of 18:25 and 18:29.

verses.text: When the righteous turns from his righteousness and commits iniquity, he will even die therein.
verses.arminianNotes: “When the righteous turns from his righteousness and commits iniquity, he will even die therein.” Arminian readers see a real possibility that one who was truly righteous may turn to iniquity and perish. The wider question of falling away is treated at Hebrews 6:4 and Hebrews 6:6, and is not settled here.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hold either that those who finally fall away were not truly regenerate, or that the warning is a real means God uses to keep his people persevering. Shared ground: both traditions hear the warning as serious; the wider question of falling away is treated at Hebrews 6:4 and Hebrews 6:6, and is not settled here.

verses.text: When the wicked turns from his wickedness and does that which is lawful and right, he will live by it.
verses.arminianNotes: “When the wicked turns from his wickedness and does that which is lawful and right, he will live by it.” Arminian readers see the door of mercy open again: the turning God calls for is a real response, enabled and invited by grace.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the promise of life to the one who turns, and they see the turning itself as the fruit of grace at work. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as pairing with 33:18, so that the outcome follows the direction a person’s life finally takes.

verses.text: Yet you say, “The way of the Lord is not fair.” House of Israel, I will judge every one of you after his ways.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The people repeat, “The way of the Lord is not fair”, and the LORD replies, “I will judge every one of you after his ways.” Arminian readers see judgment by each person’s conduct joined to the call of 33:11, so that no one is left without a way to turn.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD affirming his own justice and the personal accountability of each hearer. Shared ground: both traditions read the closing verse, like 18:30, as a summons to take one’s own ways seriously rather than blame God.
